new mexico.damages_note: The jury may award compensatory and exemplary (punitive) damages it deems fair and just, based on the financial loss to the survivors, including medical and funeral expenses, lost earnings and benefits, household services, loss of guidance and counsel, the value of the life itself, and the decedent's pain and suffering before death. There is no damages cap in the Wrongful Death Act itself. Proceeds are not subject to the decedent's debts and are divided in a fixed order set by the statute.
new mexico.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death (N.M. Stat. Ann. § 41-2-2). Claims against a government body are different: written notice is generally due within 6 months of the injury that caused the death, and suit within 2 years under the Tort Claims Act.
new mexico.state_note: New Mexico is unusual in letting the jury award damages for the value of the deceased person's life itself, not just measurable financial losses; and family members can never file in their own names — only the personal representative can.
new mexico.who_can_file: Only the personal representative (executor or administrator) of the deceased person's estate may bring the claim, and it is brought in the representative's name for the benefit of the statutory beneficiaries: the surviving spouse, children and grandchildren, then the parents of a deceased minor, then siblings (N.M. Stat. Ann. § 41-2-3).

new york.damages_note: Only pecuniary (financial) losses may be recovered: lost financial support, lost services, loss of parental guidance, lost inheritance, plus medical expenses and funeral costs, with interest from the date of death. Grief, sorrow and loss of companionship are NOT recoverable. Punitive damages are allowed where the decedent could have recovered them (EPTL § 5-4.3). No cap on compensatory damages.
new york.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death; 2 years and 6 months for deaths caused by the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. If a criminal case was filed over the same event, the personal representative gets at least 1 year from the end of the criminal case. Claims against a city, town or county need a notice of claim within 90 days.
new york.state_note: New York is one of the few states that bars grief and loss-of-companionship damages entirely; the Grieving Families Act that would have allowed them was vetoed on December 5, 2025, and a 2026 bill remains in committee. Note the Legal Aid Society serves New York City; upstate residents should use LawHelpNY to find their local program.
new york.who_can_file: Only the duly appointed personal representative of the deceased person's estate may bring the claim, for the benefit of the distributees — the surviving spouse, children, parents, siblings and other heirs in the order set by inheritance law (N.Y. Est. Powers & Trusts Law § 5-4.1).

north carolina.damages_note: Medical and hospital expenses, the decedent's pain and suffering before death, funeral expenses, and the present monetary value of the decedent to the family — lost net income, services, protection, care, society, companionship, comfort, guidance and advice. Punitive damages are allowed for malice or willful or wanton conduct, capped at the greater of 3 times compensatory damages or $250,000. No general cap on compensatory damages. The recovery is generally not liable for the decedent's debts, except burial expenses and up to $4,500 in medical expenses.
north carolina.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1-53) — shorter than North Carolina's 3-year deadline for most personal-injury claims. Exceptions are rare, such as tolling while a beneficiary is a minor or fraudulent concealment of the cause of death.
north carolina.state_note: North Carolina is one of the few states with pure contributory negligence: if the person who died was even 1% at fault for the accident, the family may recover nothing.
north carolina.who_can_file: Only the personal representative (or collector) of the deceased person's estate may bring the claim, for the benefit of the surviving spouse, children, parents and other heirs under intestacy law (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 28A-18-2).

north dakota.damages_note: Damages proportionate to the injury to those entitled to recover, including lost income and financial support, household services, medical and funeral expenses, and loss of society and companionship. No general cap on damages; a $500,000 cap on non-economic damages applies only to medical-malpractice cases, and punitive damages are capped at the greater of 2 times compensatory damages or $250,000. The recovery is exempt from the decedent's debts and goes to the heirs at law.
north dakota.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (N.D. Cent. Code § 28-01-18(4)). If the death resulted from medical malpractice, the deadline is 2 years from when the malpractice was discovered, but no more than 6 years from when it happened.
north dakota.state_note: Unlike most states, North Dakota lets surviving family members file the claim themselves in a fixed priority order, rather than only through the estate's personal representative — and the recovery is protected from the decedent's creditors.
north dakota.statute_name: North Dakota Death by Wrongful Act
north dakota.who_can_file: The claim must be brought by the following people, in this order: the surviving spouse, then the surviving children, then the surviving mother or father, then a surviving grandparent, then the personal representative of the estate, then a person who had primary physical custody of the decedent. If the person first in line refuses or neglects to file for 30 days after a demand from the next person in line, that next person may file (N.D. Cent. Code § 32-21-03).

ohio.damages_note: Loss of financial support, loss of services, loss of society, companionship, care, guidance and counsel, loss of prospective inheritance, mental anguish suffered by surviving family members, and funeral and burial expenses. There is no cap on compensatory damages. Punitive damages are not listed among wrongful-death damages in the statute.
ohio.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (Ohio Rev. Code § 2125.02(D)(1)). Product-liability wrongful-death claims have a 10-year statute of repose with exceptions, and deaths from prolonged exposure to a product must be filed within 2 years of learning the cause of death.
ohio.state_note: Ohio is one of the few states that expressly lets surviving family members recover for their own mental anguish, and since a 2023 amendment, other next of kin who want a share must file a notice of claim with the probate court within 2 years of the death.
ohio.who_can_file: The personal representative of the deceased person's estate must bring the claim, for the exclusive benefit of the surviving spouse, children and parents (who are presumed to have suffered damages) and other next of kin (Ohio Rev. Code § 2125.02).

oklahoma.damages_note: Medical and burial expenses; loss of consortium and grief of the surviving spouse; the decedent's mental pain and anguish before death; pecuniary loss to the survivors; and grief and loss of companionship of the decedent's children and parents. Punitive (exemplary) damages may be recovered in proper cases. For the death of an unmarried, unemancipated minor child, damages also include loss of companionship and love, destruction of the parent-child relationship, and support and education costs (§ 1055).
oklahoma.deadline_note: 2 years from the death. Claims against a government entity need a written notice of claim within 1 year of the death under the Governmental Tort Claims Act.
oklahoma.state_note: Oklahoma's statute is unusual in two ways: it spells out damages beneficiary by beneficiary in the statute itself, and it also covers the death of an unborn person (§ 1053(F)).
oklahoma.who_can_file: The personal representative of the deceased person's estate brings the claim. If the decedent was a nonresident, or a resident with no personal representative appointed, the widow — or, if there is no widow, the next of kin — may bring it instead (Okla. Stat. tit. 12, §§ 1053–1054).

oregon.damages_note: Reasonable medical, hospital, nursing, burial and memorial expenses; the decedent's pain, suffering, disability and lost income between injury and death; pecuniary loss to the estate; and loss of society, companionship and services for the spouse, children, stepchildren, stepparents and parents. Punitive damages are allowed where the decedent could have recovered them. Non-economic damages are generally capped at $500,000 (ORS 31.710), with exceptions; economic damages are uncapped.
oregon.deadline_note: 3 years after the injury that caused the death is discovered or reasonably should have been discovered, but never later than 3 years after the death (or the longest applicable statute of ultimate repose).
oregon.state_note: Oregon's clock runs from discovery of the injury, not just from the death, but is capped at 3 years after death — and stepchildren and stepparents are expressly included as beneficiaries even if they would not inherit under intestacy law.
oregon.who_can_file: Only the personal representative of the deceased person's estate may bring the claim, for the benefit of the surviving spouse, surviving children, surviving parents, stepchildren and stepparents, and anyone else who would inherit the decedent's personal property under intestacy law (Or. Rev. Stat. § 30.020).

pennsylvania.damages_note: Reasonable hospital, nursing, medical and funeral expenses and estate administration expenses, plus lost financial support, household services, society, comfort and guidance. No cap on compensatory damages. Punitive damages are generally not available in the wrongful-death action itself, though they may be available in a companion survival action (42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8302). Only a spouse, child or parent can benefit; if none survive, only special damages may be recovered.
pennsylvania.deadline_note: 2 years from the date of death (42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 5524(2)). Claims against a government entity require notice within 6 months of the death.
pennsylvania.state_note: Only a spouse, child or parent can recover under the Wrongful Death Act — siblings and unmarried partners cannot. Also, the separate survival action (for the decedent's own pre-death pain and suffering) runs on a different clock, from the date of injury rather than the date of death. Note: the Legal Aid Network is a statewide network that refers callers to the legal-aid program serving their county; it does not represent clients directly.
pennsylvania.who_can_file: The personal representative of the estate has the exclusive right to file for the first 6 months after the death. If the personal representative does not file within 6 months, any beneficiary — the surviving spouse, child or parent — may file on behalf of all beneficiaries (Pa. R. Civ. P. 2202; 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8301).

rhode island.damages_note: Pecuniary losses such as lost future income and household services, medical and funeral expenses, the decedent's pain and suffering before death, and loss of consortium, society and companionship — including emotional distress and grief — for a spouse, children or parents. Punitive damages are available where the decedent could have recovered them (§ 10-7-7.1). Rhode Island guarantees a minimum recovery of $350,000 when liability is found (raised from $250,000 effective January 1, 2024).
rhode island.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death. If the wrongful act that caused the death was not known at the time of death, the deadline is 3 years from when it was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered (R.I. Gen. Laws § 10-7-2(c)).
rhode island.state_note: Rhode Island is rare in guaranteeing a minimum $350,000 recovery in a successful wrongful-death case, and it expressly lets a spouse, child or parent sue separately for loss of companionship and emotional distress.
rhode island.statute_name: Rhode Island Death by Wrongful Act
rhode island.who_can_file: The executor or administrator of the deceased person's estate has the exclusive right to file for the first 6 months after the death. If no executor or administrator files within 6 months (or there is none), the beneficiaries may file on behalf of all beneficiaries (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 10-7-2, 10-7-3). Separately, a surviving spouse, child or parent may bring their own claim for loss of consortium, society and companionship (§ 10-7-1.2).

south carolina.damages_note: The jury may award damages proportioned to the injury to the beneficiaries: lost income and benefits, household services, medical and funeral expenses, loss of companionship, guidance, care and protection, and mental anguish. Exemplary (punitive) damages are allowed for recklessness, wilfulness or malice, capped at the greater of 3 times compensatory damages or $500,000 (up to 4 times or $2,000,000 in defined cases). Any settlement of a wrongful-death or survival action must be approved by a probate, circuit or federal court.
south carolina.deadline_note: 3 years from the date of death (S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530(6)). Claims against government entities have much shorter deadlines, often measured in months.
south carolina.state_note: A child's right to benefit is not affected by the parents' marital status (§ 15-51-30), and every settlement of a wrongful-death claim needs court approval — families cannot settle privately without a judge signing off.
south carolina.statute_name: South Carolina Death by Wrongful Act Statute
south carolina.who_can_file: Only the executor or administrator of the deceased person's estate may bring the claim, for the benefit of the surviving spouse and children first, then the parents, then the heirs (S.C. Code Ann. §§ 15-51-10, 15-51-20).
